title: Effects of weather on the performance of marathon runners
population: Stockholm Marathon 1980-2008 (annual finishing-time anomaly after removing the linear trend), male and female runners including slower finishers up to 4.7 h, plus percentage of non-finishers
findings: Air temperature had the highest correlation with finishing-time anomaly in all categories (r = 0.66-0.73, highest for the slowest runners).

Solar shortwave radiation (r = 0.41-0.71), relative humidity (r = -0.57 to -0.44) and, for men, rain (r = -0.51 to -0.42) were also significantly correlated, but humidity and rain effects arose only from their negative correlation with air temperature.
Percentage of non-finishers was significantly affected by air temperature and specific humidity (r = 0.72, multiple regression).

Slower runners were more affected by unfavourable weather than faster runners (previously shown for 2.1-3 h finishers, now extended to 4.7 h); warm-weather effects were less evident for women, 'probably partly' due to larger surface-area-to-mass ratio and slower speed.
limitations: One race, about 29 annual aggregates (1980-2008, count is arithmetic), humidity and rain confounded with temperature; anomaly depends on the detrending method; the sex difference is speculative per the author.
implications: Include solar radiation alongside temperature (r up to 0.71), supporting WBGT or globe-temperature input over air temperature alone.
Use specific (absolute) humidity, not relative humidity, for DNF or withdrawal-risk warnings.
Scale heat penalties up for slower runners (evidence to about 4.7 h finishing times); beyond that extrapolation is unsupported.
No sex-specific penalty is justified on this evidence.

verification.notes: Crossref gives online 2009-11-25, print 2010-05; issue year 2010 used. Abstract (PMID 19937453) re-fetched; added the rain correlation and the 'probably partly' wording. All numbers match.
